sens: Chief of the Merarites, one of the three major families of Levites
H6700.detail: Tsuriel is a Levite from the tribe of the Merarites (descendants of Merari, son of Levi). At the time of the Exodus, he is appointed chief of his paternal house, meaning he is responsible for an important family branch. His role involves leading the Merarites during the encampment and movements of the people in the desert (Numbers 3:35). The three families of Levites — Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites — shared the responsibilities of the tabernacle service; the Merarites were in charge of the framework and bars of the sanctuary.
H6700.origine: The name Tsuriel means "my rock is God": it is composed of "tsour" (rock, refuge) and the divine name "El". It is a very common theophoric name in the Bible, where "rock" designates God as a solid and unshakeable foundation. The name reflects the trust in God that parents wish to convey.
H6700.emploi: Tsuriel appears only once in the entire Bible, in Numbers 3:35. This passage lists the chiefs of the three major branches of Levites during the census at Sinai, a few weeks after the exodus from Egypt. Tsuriel is presented there as the son of Abihail and chief of the families of Merari. It is a foundational moment: Moses organizes the worship service by assigning each chief their specific responsibility.
H6700.portee: The testimony of Tsuriel reminds us that God entrusts concrete responsibilities to ordinary men. Although very little known and mentioned only once, Tsuriel had an important place in the people of God: to make worship function and serve the community. This encourages the believer to accept the tasks they receive, whether great or small.

sens: Father of Shelumiel, chief of the tribe of Simeon at the time of the Exodus
H6701.detail: Tsurischaddaï is a man whose name is mentioned in the Bible only through his son Shelumiel. He is the father of Shelumiel, who is designated as the chief or prince of the tribe of Simeon during the census and organization of the people of Israel in the desert (Numbers 1:6). His name appears every time Shelumiel is presented in his functions: at the time of the census of the tribes, during the establishment of the camp, and when Shelumiel presents the offerings of his tribe to the Lord (Numbers 7:36-41). Although Tsurischaddaï himself is never an actor in the narrative, he is mentioned as a genealogical reference and as an example of the family and tribal structure of the people of God at that time.
H6701.origine: The name Tsurischaddaï literally means "my rock is the Almighty": it is composed of two Hebrew elements, "tsur" (rock, fortress) and "Shaddaï" (Almighty, divine name). This name reveals the faith of Shelumiel's father: it expresses trust in God as an unshakeable rock and as sovereign strength. It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the name or a quality of God, which was common among the Hebrews to express their piety.
H6701.emploi: Tsurischaddaï is named five times in the book of Numbers, always in relation to his son Shelumiel. He appears during the first census of Israel at Sinai (Numbers 1:6), in the organization of the camp of the tribes (Numbers 2:12), and three times during the dedication of the Tabernacle when Shelumiel presents the offerings and sacrifices of the tribe of Simeon (Numbers 7:36 and 7:41). He is also mentioned during the march in the desert (Numbers 10:19). His name does not appear anywhere else in the Bible. He represents an anonymous but reliable paternal figure in the genealogy and administration of the people of Israel at the time of the Exodus.

sens: Destroy by fire
Completely annihilate
H6702.detail:
1. Consume means to completely destroy by fire, to reduce to ashes. The prophet Isaiah uses this verb to say that God will walk against the thorns and thistles and will consume them all together (Isaiah 27:4): the image is that of a fire that devours and annihilates mercilessly.
2. In a figurative sense, the word evokes complete annihilation, total destruction. To consume something by fire is to put an end to it decisively and irreversibly.
H6702.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root (צ-ו-ת) that means "to burn" or "to ignite". The form used here is the Hiphil, which indicates a causative action: to cause to burn, to set on fire. This verb belongs to the same family as other Hebrew words expressing burning and destruction by fire.
H6702.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 27:4. In this prophetic text, God affirms that He has no anger against His people, but that if He encounters hostile obstacles (symbolized by thorns and thistles), He will consume them without hesitation. This context shows the verb used to express a definitive and radical destruction.
H6702.portee: This word reminds us that God can destroy evil and everything that opposes His plans with absolute efficiency. For the Christian, it evokes the certainty that nothing can resist divine power when it manifests.

sens: White, of a bright and shining color
Brilliant, luminous, dazzling
Clear, distinct, sharply perceptible
Burning, ardent (referring to heat or wind)
H6703.detail:
1. White is the lightest and purest color: it evokes brightness and distinction. Thus, in the Song of Solomon, the beloved is described as "white and ruddy," meaning resplendent and remarkable among all men (Song of Solomon 5:10).
2. The brilliant refers to what shines with a bright and dazzling light, like the heat of the sun at midday. Isaiah 18:4 speaks of the "brilliant heat of the light," an image of intense and overwhelming clarity.
3. What is clear is understood unambiguously, stands out sharply. Isaiah 32:4 says that the tongue of those who stutter will speak "clearly," meaning distinctly and intelligibly, without confusion.
4. The burning evokes a dry and scorching heat, almost violent. Jeremiah 4:11 speaks of a "burning" wind blowing from the desert, a destructive and arid force.
H6703.origine: The Hebrew word צַח comes from a root that expresses the idea of extreme clarity and purity. The basic image is that of something so clear and bright that it is almost blinding, or so ardent that it consumes. This root has few derivatives in Hebrew, which shows that this word designates a very particular and striking quality.
H6703.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible. It first describes the dazzling beauty of a person (the beloved in the Song). It then characterizes intense natural phenomena: the sunlight and the heat of a summer day, or the dry and burning wind of the desert. The word is never used neutrally: it always emphasizes an intensity that strikes, whether it is beautiful and attractive or destructive and threatening.
H6703.portee: This word reminds us that purity and brightness speak to the human heart. It also evokes the power of natural elements, the intensity of the world created by God, which can be both alluring and terrible. For the believer, it invites recognition of divine majesty in clarity and power.

sens: To be deprived of water, to become dry and arid
To suffer from extreme drought, to die of thirst
H6704.detail:
1. The word denotes the state of that which lacks water and becomes completely dry. In Isaiah 5:13, the multitude of the people becomes "dried up by thirst": it is the image of a drought that strangles, depriving of what is vital.
2. Beyond the physical sense, it expresses the suffering and death that come from lack. When a crowd is dried up by thirst in the midst of captivity, it conveys the idea of total exhaustion, of a life that is extinguishing.
H6704.origine: This Hebrew root expresses the idea of radical dryness. It paints the image of land or a living creature drained of its moisture, reduced to nothing. It is a rare word in the Bible, used to describe the devastating effect of the absence of water in an arid climate.
H6704.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 5:13. It is placed in the context of a prophetic judgment: the disobedient people of God will be taken into captivity, and those who remain will suffer from hunger and thirst. The prophet uses the stark image of desiccation to show the horror and totality of divine punishment.
H6704.portee: This word reminds us that the absence of water — a symbol of life and God's blessings — is a fearsome form of judgment. It invites the reader to grasp how captivity and distance from God represent a slow death. It is also a warning: rejecting the word of God leads to exhaustion, not to life.

sens: to shine with a white brilliance
to radiate clarity
to resplend
to appear radiant or magnificent
H6705.detail:
1. The verb describes a dazzling, white, and blinding brightness. In Lamentations 4:7, it applies to the princes of Judah: their skin shone whiter than snow or milk, so radiant and bright they were.
2. The image evokes an intense luminous glow, like that produced by the reflection of light on a white or polished surface. It is a whiteness that dazzles the eye with its purity.
3. The word can also denote a moral or prestigious radiance: it is not just being white, but shining with nobility, honor, or remarkable beauty.
H6705.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that paints the image of a dazzling brightness. This root expresses the idea of a white or luminous radiance, hence "to sparkle," "to resplend." Most ancient translations capture this notion of intense brilliance and dazzling.
H6705.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Lamentations 4:7. In this poignant text, the prophet describes the lost splendor of the people of Judah: once, the princes radiated with dazzling beauty, compared to the purity of snow, milk, or the luster of sapphire. It is a painful contrast with their present degradation, described in the following verses. The context gives the word an emotional weight: the princes' brilliance no longer exists, swallowed by misfortune.
H6705.portee: This word reminds the reader that human splendor, even the most dazzling, is fragile and can disappear. The princes once radiated; Lamentations shows that they have lost that brilliance. This invites us to place our trust not in a beauty or earthly glory that fades, but in the solidity of God, which is truly enduring.

sens: Devoid of covering or protection
Exposed to view, without protection
Smooth and shiny surface
Bare, uncovered by destruction
H6706.detail:
1. The word describes a surface devoid of what usually covers it. In Ezekiel 24:7, the spilled blood remains on the "naked rock," that is, on the bare stone, without earth or dust to hide it — the image is one of total exposure, nothing veils what is seen there.

2. It is a nakedness that renders vulnerable and visible. When Ezekiel announces that Tyre will be "a naked rock" (Ezekiel 26:4), he prophesies not only its ruin but also its complete exposure: the city will lose all its defenses and become a desolate place, laid bare to the gaze of all.

3. The word also evokes the shiny or gleaming aspect of a smooth surface: a rock polished by scraping, smooth and bare, with nothing to adorn or soften it.
H6706.origine: The Hebrew word צְחִיחַ comes from a root that designates what shines or glows. It is related to the idea of clarity and nakedness: something that, stripped of all ornament or covering, becomes visible in its raw nakedness. The root also evokes the shine of what is brought to light without a veil.
H6706.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Ezekiel (four occurrences). It always denotes a surface or place rendered bare by destruction or lack of covering. In Ezekiel 24:7-8, it characterizes the rock where blood has been shed without being able to be concealed: it is an image of accusation, the crime remains exposed. In Ezekiel 26:4 and 26:14, it depicts Tyre reduced to a "naked rock," a symbol of its total destruction and collapse — a smooth and barren rock can no longer shelter the glorious city. The word carries a connotation of judgment and desolation.
H6706.portee: This word reminds the believer that nothing can remain hidden before God. The spilled blood cannot be covered: it remains uncovered, a testimony of what has been committed. For Tyre, the nakedness of the rock is the image of judgment that strips away human pride. It is an invitation to recognize that the reality of evil and its consequences remain exposed, and that divine justice is not diverted by appearances.

sens: Dry land, devoid of water and vegetation
Region scorched by the sun, sterile and inhospitable
State of desolation and abandonment (figuratively)
H6707.detail:
1. The word denotes land that is completely dried up, without water or grass — the opposite of fertile and living land. In Psalms 68:7, the rebels "dwell in arid places," meaning burned and sterile regions, incapable of nourishing those who venture there.
2. It is the image of an area exposed to intense heat, where life struggles to emerge. Such land evokes abandonment and curse — it is where what has no value is thrown away.
3. Figuratively, aridity becomes the symbol of a life without divine blessing, of a miserable and hopeless situation. The rebels remain in this spiritual and physical dryness, while God leads His people to verdant places.
H6707.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be burned" or "to be dried up." It is related to the image of the sun scorching the land, depriving it of all moisture and fertility. This root evokes a violent action of fire or extreme heat that renders the land unusable.
H6707.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 68:7. It is found in a psalm of praise where David celebrates how God frees captives and fills widows, while the rebels remain in desolation. The use of the word "arid" emphasizes the contrast between the divine blessing reserved for the faithful people and the fate of the rebels, condemned to aridity.
H6707.portee: This word reminds us that rebellion against God leads to desolation and emptiness — a life without His blessing is sterile and fruitless. In contrast, those who turn to God and trust Him inherit fertility and abundance. It is an invitation to seek the living water that only God can give.

sens: Foul odor and repugnant smell that emanates from something decomposing
Infection or corruption that spreads
Disgust or horror (in a figurative sense)
H6709.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a foul and repulsive odor, such as that emitted by corpses or decaying matter. In Joel 2:20, the defeated enemy army will leave a stench rising to heaven — a stark image of massive death and destruction.
2. Beyond the raw odor, the word evokes corruption that contaminates and spreads: this infection from the north that "will spread" (Joel 2:20) symbolizes how evil and death invade the territory.
3. The stench also becomes a figure of moral or spiritual disgust: it expresses the horror provoked by perversion, sin, or malice.
H6709.origine: The Hebrew word צַחֲנָה comes from a root that conveys the idea of something foul, infected. It belongs to the family of Hebrew words that describe unpleasant odors and corruption. Its primary image is concrete: that of the nauseating emanations rising from putrefaction or decay.
H6709.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Joel 2:20, at the heart of the prophet Joel's vision concerning the judgment of the locusts and the army from the north that ravages Judah. Joel does not choose it by chance: by describing the stench that the corpses of these invaders will leave, he paints the extent of the disaster. The image also evokes divine judgment — when God defeats His enemies, only corruption and horror remain.
H6709.portee: This word reminds us that sin and evil bear within them the fruits of death and destruction. The stench rising from the corpses is not just a horrifying detail: it is the visible sign that those who oppose God ultimately face defeat and corruption. For the believer, it is a call not to ally with what leads to death, but to turn to the One who gives life.

sens: region dried out by heat and lack of water
state of deprivation and spiritual sterility
H6710.detail:
1. The word concretely refers to land scorched by the sun, incapable of producing, where water is sorely lacking. In Isaiah 58:11, God promises that the one who practices righteousness will be transformed: he will no longer be like a "dry land," but like a "watered garden" where water abounds and life flourishes.
2. By extension, this dryness becomes an image of the dried-up soul, spiritually impoverished, which needs the presence and grace of God to come back to life. This is why the prophet uses this contrast: God "will satisfy your soul in dry places" — meaning He will fill what was empty and barren.
H6710.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes drying, the heat that burns and desiccates. The reduplicated form (the word partially repeats) reinforces the idea of total, irreparable aridity. It is the portrait of contrast: what is dry can only live by water, just as the soul can only be transformed by God's intervention.
H6710.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 58:11. It is found in a promise of transformation: the one who fasts correctly — not for appearance, but to help the poor — will receive from God an abundant and satisfying life. The "dryness" then becomes the symbol of the selfish or empty heart before encountering God and His righteousness.
H6710.portee: This image speaks to the heart of every believer: our efforts, our personal accomplishments leave us "dry" — thirsty for meaning and true life. Only God can transform this dryness into a fruitful garden. It is a call to seek in God, not in ourselves, the source of abundant life.

sens: Laughter, expressing joy or amusement through laughter
To mock, to make fun of someone
To play, to entertain, to take pleasure
To joke, to jest, to act lightly
H6711.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply to laugh, to manifest gaiety or astonishment through laughter. Abraham laughs when God tells him he will have a son at a hundred years old (Genesis 17:17): it is a laugh of disbelief mixed with joy. Sarah also laughs upon hearing this news (Genesis 18:13), struck by the joyful absurdity of the promise.
2. The word can express mockery or ridicule. When Lot warns his sons-in-law that the city will be destroyed, he "seems to them to be joking" (Genesis 19:14): they take him for a joker, they mock him. It is a laugh that devalues, that refuses to take seriously.
3. To play, to entertain, to seek pleasure: the people of Israel at Sinai "rose up to play" around the golden calf (Exodus 32:6), not merely to laugh, but to feast, dance, celebrate carelessly.
4. To joke or jest can also mean to abuse, to play with someone maliciously. Potiphar's wife accuses Joseph of coming to "play" with her (Genesis 39:14), meaning to seduce or mock her.
H6711.origine: The Hebrew root צחק (tsachaq) expresses the idea of laughter that can be joyful, mocking, or playful. It is related to movement and release: the one who laughs lets out their amusement or nervousness. The proper name Yitshak (Isaac) derives directly from it, as Isaac means "he will laugh" or "the one who laughs," a name chosen to perpetuate the memory of Abraham and Sarah's laughter in response to the incredible promise of a child. This root appears mainly in the narratives of Genesis and in a few passages where the people engage in festivity or entertainment.
H6711.emploi: The verb צחק appears about 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Genesis. The earliest uses are those of Abraham and Sarah laughing upon learning of the miraculous birth of Isaac (Genesis 17:17; 18:12-13, 15; 21:6, 9). The laughter is mixed with surprise and joy, but also with disbelief in the face of the impossible. In Genesis 19:14, Lot is taken for a joker when he warns of the destruction of Sodom: here, the verb marks the refusal to listen, the mockery. In Genesis 39:14 and 39:17, the verb describes the accusation of "playing" with the woman, with a connotation of dishonesty. In Exodus 32:6, the people "play" during the idolatry of the golden calf: it is a carnal gaiety and religiously corrupt. The meaning thus varies between joyful laughter, mockery, carefree play, and malicious seduction.
H6711.portee: This word reminds us that laughter traverses the entire human experience: it can express joy and trust in God (as with Abraham and Sarah discovering the promise), but also disbelief, mockery, and a lack of fear of God. The Christian is invited to discern the quality of laughter: that which arises from faith and wonder, or that which closes its eyes to the truth. The name Isaac perpetuates this memory, reminding each generation that what seems impossible to humans is possible with God.

sens: action of laughing, manifestation of joy through laughter
that which makes one laugh or becomes a subject of mockery and ridicule
H6712.detail:
1. Laughter is the natural expression of joy or gladness. Sarah, having become a mother at an old age, exclaims: "God has made me laugh" (Genesis 21:6), meaning that all who hear of her pregnancy will laugh with joy alongside her, as the event seems wonderful and incredible.
2. The word also refers to one who becomes the object of others' laughter, that is, the subject of ridicule or mockery. In Ezekiel 23:32, the bitter cup will make the woman "an object of ridicule and mockery": she will be exposed to scorn, publicly humiliated by her fate. Here, laughter becomes a weapon of contempt.
H6712.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of playing, laughing, or mocking. It is related to the notion of play and lightness. In biblical Hebrew, laughter can express both innocent joy and malicious laughter; the context determines the nuance. The word appears in different forms to designate either the act of laughing or the ridiculed person.
H6712.emploi: This Hebrew word appears only twice in the provided biblical text. In Genesis 21:6, it evokes the sincere and contagious joy that results from the fulfillment of a divine promise: the birth of Isaac. In Ezekiel 23:32, it takes on a negative tone and denotes the humiliation of being the target of mockery. These two usages show that biblical laughter can be an expression of divine blessing (laughter of joy) or an indication of a fall (laughter of derision). The prophetic context of Ezekiel emphasizes judgment: laughter becomes a symbol of shame.
H6712.portee: This word reminds us that laughter is a gift from God, an expression of His joy and blessings. But it also warns us that ridicule and mockery are formidable forms of humiliation. For the believer, it is a call to seek the joyful laughter that the Lord provides rather than fearing the scorn of men, and to never use laughter to hurt or despise others.

sens: wool of white or very light color
highly valued merchandise in ancient trade
H6713.detail:
1. White wool is natural unbleached wool, of very light or bright color. It is a precious material in biblical times, particularly sought after for the fineness and purity of its hue. In Ezekiel 27:18, Damascus supplies Tyre with white wool as one of its most prestigious goods, alongside the wine of Helbon.
2. This type of wool represents a luxury product and highly valued trade item in the economy of the ancient Levant. The mention of white wool underscores the wealth of commercial exchanges between cities: it was a sought-after good that attested to the prosperity and importance of the cities that produced it.
H6713.origine: The Hebrew word צַחַר (tsachar) literally means "reddish-gray" or "tawny," but here it refers to white or very light wool, probably from fine-breed sheep raised in Syria. The etymology suggests a natural color or a particular bleaching process. The word belongs to the domain of commerce and textiles in the Old Testament.
H6713.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:18. The context is one of lamentation over Tyre, a great maritime commercial power. The detailed enumeration of goods that various regions supplied to Tyre illustrates the economic importance of this city and its commercial prominence. The white wool from Damascus is listed as one of the prestigious products, testifying to the quality and reputation of Syrian textile production.
H6713.portee: This passage shows how material wealth and prosperous trade characterized the powers of the ancient world. For the Christian reader, it invites reflection on the ephemeral nature of earthly prosperity: Tyre, despite all its commercial splendor and precious goods, will face ruin. The goods of this world, however prestigious they may be, are but vanity.

sens: Father of Ephron the Hittite, owner of the field of Machpelah
Son of Ashur and Helah, in the genealogy of Judah
H6714G.detail:
1. Tsochar is the father of Ephron the Hittite, who sells Abraham the field and cave of Machpelah to bury Sarah (Genesis 23:8; 25:9). He is a man from the time of the Patriarchs, mentioned because his son plays an important role in the story of Abraham.
2. Another Tsochar appears in the genealogy of the sons of Ashur within the tribe of Judah: he is the son of Helah (1 Chronicles 4:7). The Bible mentions him simply in the list of descendants, without detail about his life.
H6714G.origine: The name Tsochar means "tawny" or "color tawny," possibly evoking a notable physical appearance. It is a simple Hebrew name, formed from a root designating a hue or color. Two different men bear this name in the biblical texts: one in the time of Abraham, the other among the descendants of Ashur in Judah.
H6714G.emploi: Tsochar appears three times in the Bible. Twice he is identified as the father of Ephron the Hittite, the owner of the field of Machpelah near Hebron: Abraham addresses Ephron by calling him "Ephron, son of Tsochar" (Genesis 23:8), and later the narrator recalls that the field belonged to "Ephron, son of Tsochar, the Hittite" (Genesis 25:9). A third mention places him in the genealogy of Judah, among the sons of Ashur and Helah (1 Chronicles 4:7), without narrative context. This Tsochar is likely a different person from the father of Ephron.

sens: Son of Simeon, one of the twelve ancestors of Israel
H6714H.detail: 1. Tsochar is one of the sons of Simeon and the grandson of Jacob. He appears in the genealogical lists that enumerate the children of Simeon during the descent into Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:10) and again in the account of the census in the wilderness (Exodus 6:15). His name is also borne by other individuals in the Old Testament — notably Zerah, a descendant of Judah — but this one is specifically the son of Simeon and the Canaanite woman.
H6714H.origine: The name Tsochar means "reddish" or "tawny" in Hebrew, probably a physical description. This same name appears elsewhere in the form Zerah (זֶרַח), which has the same meaning. Like many names of the ancestors of Israel, it reflects a visible characteristic or an image that marked the family.
H6714H.emploi: Tsochar is mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in the genealogies of the sons of Simeon: first in Genesis 46:10 when Jacob descends into Egypt with all his household, and then in Exodus 6:15 during the census of the Israelites in the wilderness, before they enter Canaan. These genealogical lists establish the twelve tribes and their founding families. Tsochar is only listed in these enumerations; no specific act or word is attributed to him in the biblical text.

sens: Of pale or light color, particularly when referring to the coat of an animal
Pure, without stain, innocent
H6715.detail:
1. The word denotes a pale and light color, notably the white or cream coat of female donkeys. In Judges 5:10, the poet mentions "white donkeys" as prestigious mounts, a sign of wealth and dignity for the women who ride them — remarkable animals distinguished by their light coat and elegant appearance.
2. White also evokes moral purity and innocence: one who is white of guilt is blameless, washed of all fault. This image of immaculate white, free from stain, runs throughout Scripture.
H6715.origine: The Hebrew word צָחֹר (tsahor) is related to roots that express brightness and clarity. Its primary image is that of a shiny, clear surface that reflects light. In biblical language, white naturally becomes the symbol of what is pure, intact, and radiant.
H6715.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 5:10, in the Song of Deborah. It qualifies the donkeys of high-ranking women who join in the celebration of victory. The context shows that these white mounts are a sign of status and wealth, not mere pack animals but remarkable creatures noted for their apparent beauty.
H6715.portee: For the believer, the white of the donkeys in Judges 5:10 reminds us that even the material and visible details of our lives — our possessions, our appearance, our responsibilities — can testify to the glory of God and our commitment to His cause. The purity that shines in the eyes of men must first reign in the heart.

sens: Sea vessel intended for transport or warfare
Means of crossing rivers and seas
Symbol of military or political power
H6716.detail:
1. A ship is a large boat built for navigating the sea. In Isaiah 33:21, the text speaks of "oared ships" and "great vessels" that cross rivers: it is the image of a ship equipped for maritime navigation.
2. By extension, the ship refers to any vessel capable of crossing large bodies of water, rivers, or seas. It is a means of transport and communication between peoples, particularly important for the commercial and military empires of antiquity.
3. Finally, the ship carries a political and military dimension: the "ships of Kittim" (Numbers 24:24; Daniel 11:30) represent the military power of the empires that send them. When Daniel 11:30 speaks of "discouraged ships," it indicates that these ships symbolize the army and the will to conquer of a powerful king.
H6716.origine: The Hebrew word צִי (tsi) denotes the ship as a vessel. It belongs to a maritime lexical field and recalls the importance of trade and navigation in the biblical world. In ancient Greek, we find ναῦς (naús), which directly means "boat" or "ship." The word emphasizes the material infrastructure of the political and commercial power of peoples.
H6716.emploi: The word "ship" appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used in major prophetic contexts: in Balaam's prophecy (Numbers 24:24), where ships of Kittim (probably Cypriot or Mediterranean ships) will humiliate the Assyrian; in Isaiah's vision of protected Jerusalem (Isaiah 33:21), where no great vessel can penetrate the waters of the city; in the announcement of judgment on Egypt (Ezekiel 30:9), where ships bring terror; and in Daniel's prophecy (Daniel 11:30) where the ships of Kittim demoralize a powerful king. Each time, the ship evokes military power or mastery of maritime routes.
H6716.portee: For the biblical reader, the ship reminds us that political and military power rests on concrete material realities — mastery of the seas, armadas, navigation technology. But the Bible places these ships under God's control: it is God who sends the ships of Kittim to humiliate the Assyrian, it is God who protects Jerusalem by turning the waters into walls where no vessel can navigate. Recognizing the ship as a sign of earthly power helps the believer see that all human power, even formidable, remains subject to divine will.

sens: Servant of the house of Saul
Administrator of Mephibosheth's property
Cunning man who deceives King David
H6717.detail:
1. Tsiba is a servant of the royal house of Saul, first mentioned when David seeks to find someone from Saul's family to show kindness to (2 Samuel 9:2). He is a man in the service of a great house, tasked with domestic and administrative duties.
2. David charges him with cultivating the land and managing the harvests for Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, thus becoming his chief steward; Tsiba himself oversees fifteen sons and twenty servants who assist him in this management (2 Samuel 9:10).
3. During David's flight from Absalom, Tsiba meets the king with generous provisions and falsely accuses his master Mephibosheth of rebellion, which turns out to be partially false — revealing an opportunistic nature (2 Samuel 16:1-3).
H6717.origine: The name means "statue" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking the idea of a solid and lasting presence. Tsiba is a historical figure from the time of the united monarchy in Israel, living under Saul and David.
H6717.emploi: Tsiba appears in four major accounts in 2 Samuel. First, David identifies him as a servant of Saul and charges him to serve Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:2-12). Then, Tsiba brings provisions to David during the flight from Absalom and falsely denounces Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 16:1-4). Finally, he reappears during David's return, accompanied by many sons and servants (2 Samuel 19:17, 29). The character evolves from a simple faithful administrator to a man who exploits the situation to gain favor with the king.
H6717.portee: Tsiba illustrates how opportunism and dishonesty can corrupt even those who enjoy responsibilities and benefits. His story invites the reader to vigilance: those who serve us are not always sincere, and accusations must be evaluated with discernment, without being blinded by appearances or conventions.

sens: Wild game hunted for food
The act of hunting this wild animal
One who hunts, the hunter
H6718A.detail:
1. Game refers to the meat of a wild animal killed during hunting for food. It was a prized food in ancient life: Isaac loves Esau because he brings him tasty game, and this dish helps Jacob obtain the paternal blessing by making his father believe he has hunted it himself (Genesis 25:28 and 27:19).
2. The word also refers to the very act of hunting these animals, the practice of hunting: Esau goes out to "hunt game" and returns with his catch (Genesis 27:5, 27:30).
3. By extension, it names the one who hunts, the hunter: Nimrod is famous as a "mighty hunter before the Lord," meaning a renowned and powerful hunter (Genesis 10:9).
H6718A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to hunt" or "to track." It is related to the idea of pursuing and capturing a wild animal. In biblical Hebrew, the root evokes the dynamic action of pursuing prey in the fields or nature. The word encompasses both the activity (hunting), the result (the game brought), and the agent (the hunter).
H6718A.emploi: This word appears mainly in the narrative of Genesis where it structures the story of Isaac and his sons. Esau is presented as a good hunter who brings game to his father (Genesis 25:27-28), while Jacob, a shepherd and simple man, must use cunning to obtain the blessing by simulating this quality. The word recurs at each stage of the trap set by Rebecca (Genesis 27:3, 5, 7, 19, 25, 30-33). It also appears once in Leviticus 17:13 regarding the blood of the hunted game, and in Proverbs 12:27 where one who does not hunt wastes what he hunts, an image of laziness.
H6718A.portee: This word reminds us that ancient life depended on natural resources and the work of hunting. Esau, the hunter, represents a form of physical and practical excellence, but the narrative shows that this strength alone is not enough against cunning and God's plan. For the reader, game symbolizes the gifts received from others: Isaac blesses the one who brings him food and care, highlighting the value of service and generosity within the family.

sens: What one eats to survive, provisions and supplies
Food that is brought along or stored
What nourishes an animal
H6718B.detail:
1. Food primarily refers to what one eats daily to live: bread, fruits, meat. At the feet of the Gibeonites, there was dry bread that served as travel food (Joshua 9:5). It is the sustenance for the body.
2. The word is also used for provisions that are transported or accumulated — reserves for a journey or in anticipation of famine. The Israelites take provisions before going into battle (Joshua 9:14). It is the food set aside, stored up.
3. By extension, the word designates what nourishes any living being, human or animal. God provides pasture for the raven that cries out in hunger (Job 39:3). It is the food that sustains every creature.
H6718B.origine: The Hebrew word צַיִד (tsayid) comes from a root meaning "to hunt" or "to procure by hunting." Food was initially what the hunter brought back. The word retains this concrete sense of sustenance, of what one procures to live. In Aramaic, a related form also carries the meaning of "provision."
H6718B.emploi: This word appears five times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in historical narratives (Joshua, Nehemiah) and poems (Job, Psalms). It is used for travel provisions (Joshua), the trade of goods (Nehemiah 13:15), and the food that God provides for creatures (Job, Psalms). The meaning remains constant: it is always what sustains, what fills the belly. It never designates a specific food (like "bread" or "meat"), but the general idea of nourishment.
H6718B.portee: This word reminds us of a simple yet fundamental truth: every living being depends on food. God nourishes His creatures, from the hungry raven to the poor man. For a believer, this signifies that God provides, and one should not fear lack if they trust Him. It is also an invitation to remember those without provisions, those who lack the essentials.

sens: one who tracks and captures wild animals
one who pursues and captures someone
H6719.detail:
1. The hunter is primarily one who tracks wild animals to capture or kill them. He is a man who knows the techniques of hunting: he sets traps, uses weapons, follows the tracks of his prey. In Jeremiah 16:16, the Lord speaks of sending "hunters" who will pursue the inhabitants of the land as one hunts game: an image of relentless pursuit, impossible to escape.
2. By extension, the hunter designates anyone who pursues someone to capture or punish them. The term applies to the merciless pursuit of a person, with the idea that the prey cannot escape. This is the image developed by the prophet: the Judeans will be hunted in the mountains and rocks, like game fleeing from hunters.
H6719.origine: The Hebrew word צַיָּד (tsayad) comes from the root צ-י-ד which means "to hunt," "to trap." This root evokes the action of setting traps and capturing by cunning or force. The word designates both the hunter and the hunt itself. It is an ancient biblical image: the patriarchs and kings of Israel hunt for their food, and hunting often symbolizes pursuit, capture, or God's judgment on enemies.
H6719.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 16:16. It is used in a context of prophetic judgment: God announces that He will first send "fishers" to capture the inhabitants (an image of easy capture or the first wave of conquest), then "hunters" to track those who might have escaped into the mountains and rocky refuges (an image of complete pursuit, the inevitability of judgment). This passage employs hunting as a metaphor for divine judgment: no one will be able to flee.
H6719.portee: The word hunter reminds us that before God, no escape is possible. It is a severe image, but it also teaches the certainty of divine judgment and the futility of resisting His will. For the believer, it invites one not to flee from God, but to come to Him with confidence, since fleeing is in vain.

sens: Food and supplies taken for a journey or an undertaking
Supplies of an army or a group on the move
Figuratively: that which supports and nourishes
H6720.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of food or provisions carried along for the journey. When Joseph orders his servants to fill his brothers' sacks, he gives them provisions for the return trip to Egypt (Genesis 42:25). This is what needs to be prepared before setting out: Joshua commands the people to gather supplies before crossing the Jordan to conquer the land (Joshua 1:11).
2. The word also applies to the supplies of an army or a troop on the move. During Gideon's battle against the Midianites, the people's provisions are taken along with the trumpets (Judges 7:8), which shows that provisions are essential for a military expedition.
3. In a figurative or spiritual sense, this word can evoke what nourishes the soul: the psalmist speaks of the bread from heaven as the "provisions" that the Lord has given (Psalms 78:25), an image of the miraculous manna that sustains the people in the desert.
H6720.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of hunting and plunder. It initially designates what one procures for sustenance, hence the meaning of food reserves. The same root produces other words related to food and what sustains life. The basic image is that of what is gathered and taken along.
H6720.emploi: This word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical accounts of the Old Testament. It is used during exoduses or significant movements: the sons of Israel in Egypt (Genesis 42:25, 45:21), the exodus from Egypt without provisions taken (Exodus 12:39), the conquest of the Jordan (Joshua 1:11), the Gibeonite ambassadors (Joshua 9:11), armies on campaign (Judges 7:8, 20:10). The word always emphasizes the importance of material preparation before a major step. A figurative occurrence in Psalms 78:25 applies the term to heavenly manna.
H6720.portee: This word reminds us that concrete life requires foresight and preparation: before embarking on a difficult path, one must equip oneself with what is necessary. For the believer, it evokes how God provides for our material needs and how we must wisely prepare for the trials and calls He addresses to us. It is a call to combined responsibility and trust.

sens: Eldest son of Canaan, eponymous ancestor of a Phoenician city
Ancient port city of Phoenicia on the Mediterranean coast
H6721G.detail:
1. Sidon is primarily a biblical character: the eldest son of Canaan, mentioned in the genealogies of the Patriarchs (Genesis 10:15 and 1 Chronicles 1:13). He is the brother of Heth, the Jebusite, the Amorite, and other sons of Canaan. As was common in antiquity, this character gave his name to a city.
2. This city, Sidon, is a major Phoenician port city located on the Mediterranean coast, north of Tyre. It was an important commercial and cultural center of the ancient world, inhabited by the Phoenicians, a people of sailors and merchants.
H6721G.origine: The Hebrew name Tsidôn literally means "the hunt" or "hunter," evoking the image of a hunting activity. The character of Sidon, son of Canaan, appears in the early genealogies of the Bible, where the founding ancestors typically give their name to the peoples or cities that descend from them. The historical city of Sidon, established on the Phoenician coast, thus bears the name of this mythical or legendary ancestor.
H6721G.emploi: Sidon appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in genealogies: in Genesis 10:15 and in 1 Chronicles 1:13, where he is listed as the firstborn son of Canaan. The Bible does not elaborate on the character himself but simply mentions his name in the succession of Noah's descendants after the Flood. It is a genealogy that establishes the legendary origins of the Canaanite and Phoenician peoples. In the New Testament, the city of Sidon is mentioned several times as an important city, but the name of the son of Canaan does not reappear there.
H6721G.portee: This brief passage reminds us that ancient peoples, including those encountered by the Israelites, had their own origins and genealogies. For the Christian reader, this invites recognition that the Word of God establishes a complete historical framework, where all peoples descend from Noah and find their place in God's plan, long before the existence of Israel.

sens: Ancient port city and commercial center of Phoenicia on the Mediterranean coast
Maritime and mercantile power rivaling Israel
Idolatrous kingdom and center of worship to pagan gods
Target of divine judgment for its pride and idols
H6721H.detail:
1. Sidon is an ancient city of Phoenicia, located on the northern Mediterranean coast, north of Tyre. It is a prosperous port and a major center of maritime trade in the ancient world (Ezekiel 27:8 speaks of its wise navigators).
2. The Bible speaks of it as an organized and influential commercial power: it is listed among the boundaries of the Canaanite lands (Genesis 10:19) and was famous for its wealth and prominence.
3. Sidon also represents a major hub of idolatrous worship: Astarte and other pagan gods were worshipped there. The Israelites sometimes fell under the influence of these Sidonian idols (Judges 10:6), which constituted a constant temptation.
4. Because of its pride and distance from God, Sidon is the subject of severe prophetic judgments (Isaiah 23:12; Ezekiel 28:22), particularly for having supported Tyre in its rebellion against the Lord.
H6721H.origine: The name literally means "hunt" or "abundant hunting" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking the fishing resources of the coast or the skill of its inhabitants. Sidon is attested in ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts as one of the oldest Phoenician cities. The Sidonians belonged to the Phoenician civilization, known for its navigation, trade, and dissemination of idolatrous worship in the Mediterranean.
H6721H.emploi: Sidon appears 18 times in the Bible. It is first mentioned as a geographical boundary of the lands of the Canaanites (Genesis 10:19), and then regularly in connection with Tyre, its neighbor and rival. In the prophets, particularly (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), Sidon is announced as a destination of divine judgment for its commercial and religious pride. It also symbolizes idolatrous temptation: the gods of Sidon seduce the Israelites (Judges 10:6). In the New Testament, Jesus and the apostles had contacts with the Sidonian region, showing that the judgment did not completely annihilate the city.
H6721H.portee: Sidon reminds us that even the greatest powers of the world, despite their wealth and influence, are under God's judgment if they forget Him and turn to idols. The repeated mention of its gods denounces the illusion that other religions could rival the worship of the true God. Finally, the prophesied judgment on Sidon shows that God controls the history of nations, including distant maritime powers.

sens: Ancient port city of Phoenicia, on the Mediterranean coast
H6721I.detail: Sidon is a major coastal city of the Phoenicians, located north of Tyre on the Mediterranean. In the provided biblical texts, it appears as a major geographical landmark: in Joshua 11:8, it is referred to as "great Sidon" during the conquest of the territory, and in Joshua 19:28, it again serves as a boundary for the lands allotted to Zebulun. It was one of the most important and oldest cities of the ancient Levant.
H6721I.origine: The name Sidon means "hunt" in Hebrew, reflecting the economic activity of this trading and port city. It is one of the oldest Phoenician cities, a major center of Mediterranean trade.
H6721I.emploi: Sidon appears twice in the provided biblical contexts, both in the context of territorial delimitation during the conquest of Canaan under Joshua. It is mentioned as "great" Sidon, highlighting its strategic and political importance. These two occurrences place it beyond the borders of Israel, serving as a landmark to define the boundaries of the lands promised to Israel.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Sidon, in Phoenicia
Trading and seafaring people of the Mediterranean coast
People known for their skill in working with cedar wood
People associated with idolatry and Canaanite gods
H6722.detail:
1. The Sidonians are the inhabitants of Sidon, a major coastal city in Phoenicia (modern-day Lebanon), located north of Tyre. They are one of the peoples that the Israelites encounter in Canaan and whom they must fight to take possession of the land (Joshua 13:6, Judges 10:12).
2. The Sidonians are renowned throughout antiquity as excellent sailors and traders. When King David and his son Solomon want to build the temple, they call upon Sidonian workers, particularly because no Israelite possesses their expertise in wood (1 Kings 5:6, 1 Chronicles 22:4).
3. Sidon is an important maritime and commercial power, and the Sidonians embody the wealth and prestige of Phoenicia. However, the Bible also presents them as idolatrous peoples, worshiping gods like Astarte (1 Kings 11:5) and Baal, which poses a spiritual threat to Israel.
H6722.origine: The Hebrew word צִידוֹנִי (Sidonian) derives from the name of the city צִידוֹן (Sidon, H6721). Sidon is one of the oldest Phoenician cities, famous since antiquity for its maritime trade and artisans. The demonym "Sidonian" simply refers to the inhabitants or nationals of this city.
H6722.emploi: The term "Sidonians" appears about 15 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, Kings, Chronicles) and in the prophet Ezekiel. It refers either to the inhabitants of Sidon whom the Israelites confront militarily, or to the skilled artisans and workers that the Israelite kings employ. The passages show that the Sidonians are both military rivals (Joshua 13:6, Judges 10:12), respected trade partners for their technical expertise (1 Kings 5:6, 1 Chronicles 22:4), and a source of idolatrous seduction, notably through Queen Jezebel, daughter of a Sidonian king, who leads Israel into the worship of Baal (1 Kings 16:31).
H6722.portee: The Sidonians remind readers that God's people do not live in isolation, but in constant contact with neighboring civilizations endowed with skills and wealth. The Bible shows that receiving material services from idolatrous peoples carries a spiritual risk: Israel may adopt their gods and practices. The example of Solomon, who allies with the Sidonians and then is seduced by their deities, illustrates how commercial and cultural compromise can lead to a diversion of faith.

sens: Lack of water, absence of moisture in the soil
Region devoid of vegetation and water
State of desiccation, drying out
Absence or deprivation (figurative sense)
H6723.detail:
1. Aridity primarily refers to the lack of water in the land: a dry soil that cannot nourish plants. Job 24:19 compares the drought and heat that absorb the water from the snow to the power of the abode of the dead.
2. It then describes a desert or arid land, meaning a region hostile to life where water is lacking. Isaiah 35:1 announces that "the desert and the arid land will rejoice," an image of transformation from misfortune to happiness.
3. Aridity can also qualify the drying out of a plant or living being, like the shoot that comes "from a dry land" in Isaiah 53:2, an image of lack of vitality.
4. Figuratively, it expresses deprivation, emptiness: Jeremiah 50:12 calls Babylon "a desert, a dry and arid land," reducing it to the desolation of judgment.
H6723.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be dry" or "to dry up." It paints the concrete image of lack of water, of cracked soil, and of dead land. It is a very ancient term that represents one of the great threats in the Near East: the desert and drought, opposed to the rain and fertility that God grants.
H6723.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and the prophets. Generally, it describes the physical state of dry land or a desert region (Isaiah 35:1, Psalms 105:41). It can also evoke the lack of water as punishment or as a sign of God's absence (Jeremiah 2:6, Jeremiah 50:12). Sometimes, it contrasts with God's promise to make water flow in arid places (Psalms 107:35, Isaiah 41:18), which becomes an image of salvation and blessing. In the prophets, aridity can also depict the desolation of a nation judged by God.
H6723.portee: For the believer, aridity reminds them of their dependence on God for water and life. It invites them to seek God "in a dry land" (Psalms 63:2), not in flight but in spiritual thirst. The promises of transformation from aridity to greenery (Isaiah 35:1) comfort those who go through the dryness of heart: only God can make the desert of their life bloom.

sens: arid terrain without water
state of extreme dryness
absence of vital resources
H6724.detail: 1. The word literally designates dry land, devoid of water and life. In Isaiah 32:2, it speaks of "streams of water in a dry place": the image is that of a region scorched by the sun, where water is lacking and where vegetation cannot survive. 2. By extension, it describes the state of extreme dryness: cracked soil, a land altered that cannot nourish one who traverses it. The striking contrast is that fresh water springs suddenly appear in the desert. 3. Figuratively, dryness becomes the image of distress or a total lack of resources: one who suffers is like abandoned in a burned land, until the Lord comes like rain or like the protective shadow over this oppressed land (Isaiah 32:2).
H6724.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of drying and aridity. It appears rarely in the Old Testament, only in the prophecies of Isaiah. The root evokes the concrete and physical image of land deprived of water, burned by the sun of the Middle Eastern desert, where water is the most precious and rare resource.
H6724.emploi: This word appears only twice in Isaiah. In Isaiah 25:5, God "subdues" or "thirsts" the heat, the image being that of a smothered fire: just as one weakens the heat by shading it, God annihilates the pride of tyrants. In Isaiah 32:2, "streams of water" miraculously spring forth "in a dry place": the image becomes comforting, promising that in the desert of distress, God will bring refreshment and life. Both uses play on the contrast: aridity and death versus water and life.
H6724.portee: For the believer, this word reminds them that the world without God is like dry land — empty of meaning, strength, and comfort. But Isaiah's promise offers hope: God is like a source of living water in the heart of the desert, refreshing the one who suffers and soothing the evil. It is a beautiful image of divine mercy towards the parched heart.

sens: Visible mark placed to indicate a location, a path, or a danger.
Monument erected to commemorate an event or a person.
Marker or signal intended to guide or alert.
H6725.detail:
1. A stone sign is a visible mark placed on the ground to signal something: a road, a danger, an important place. In Jeremiah 31:21, the prophet calls Israel to set up signs and pillars to mark the way back, like markers that guide on the road.
2. It is also a monument, that is, a structure erected to commemorate a person or an event. In 2 Kings 23:17, it is the tomb of the prophet from Judah that remains visible on the ground: a lasting sign.
3. In a darker context, it is a warning marker: in Ezekiel 39:15, when human bones are seen, a sign is placed near them until the grave diggers bury them, to signal to others that there is a dead person there.
H6725.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of marking, signaling, leaving a visible trace. The basic image is that of an object standing upright on the ground — a post, a stone, a mound — that catches the eye and communicates information from a distance. It is a sign that is seen, recognized, and that guides the one who encounters it.
H6725.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always with the concrete meaning of mark or monument. In Jeremiah 31:21, it refers to road signs that the exiles must set up to find their way back. In Ezekiel 39:15, it is an improvised grave marker. In 2 Kings 23:17, it is a lasting tomb. In all cases, it is something physical, visible, that persists and serves to inform.
H6725.portee: This word reminds us that God guides His people in a concrete and visible way. The signs set up in Jeremiah symbolize the hope of return: even scattered, Israel can find its way back. For the believer, this speaks of God's faithfulness, who does not leave His people without markers, even in exile.

sens: The fortress of Jerusalem, royal city of David
Jerusalem itself, holy city of Israel
The people of Israel and their heritage
The place of God's presence and protection
H6726.detail:
1. Zion primarily refers to the fortress that overlooks Jerusalem, the citadel that David conquered and transformed into the royal capital (2 Samuel 5:7: "David took the fortress of Zion: it is the city of David"). It is the political and military heart of the kingdom.
2. Zion becomes the poetic name for all of Jerusalem, especially in the prophets and the psalms. The two names are used together or one for the other: "Zion shall be plowed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones" (Jeremiah 26:18).
3. Zion can also refer to the people of Israel themselves and their destiny: "The remnant of Zion, the remnant of Jerusalem, shall be called holy" (Isaiah 4:3). The name evokes heritage and promise.
4. In biblical faith, Zion is the place chosen by God, where He establishes His throne and His house ("The Lord has chosen Zion," Psalms 132:13). It is the symbol of divine presence and God's blessing upon His people.
H6726.origine: The Hebrew name Zion literally means "dry place" or "arid place," likely evoking the dry and elevated rock of the hill where the fortress stands. This word quickly becomes a prestigious name, designating the royal citadel conquered by David. The Bible also uses the term "Jerusalem" (meaning "foundation of peace") to refer to the same city, but Zion emphasizes its religious, prophetic, and eschatological dimension: it is the theological heart of Israel.
H6726.emploi: Zion appears 154 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms (over 40 occurrences) and the book of Isaiah (over 40 occurrences). In the historical narratives (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), it is the fortress that David takes and where he establishes his throne. In the Psalms, Zion is celebrated as the holy mountain where God resides, where people come in pilgrimage and joy (Psalms 97:8: "Zion hears and rejoices"). In the prophets, Zion is the subject of threats of destruction (Jeremiah 26:18) and promises of glorious restoration (Isaiah 4:3; 40:9). The name concentrates Israel's eschatological hope: the place where God reigns and where His salvation is fulfilled.
H6726.portee: Zion reminds Christians that God chooses a place and a people to manifest His presence and salvation. This name reveals how God sanctifies what is ordinary — a fortress, a city — to make it a sign of His reign. For Israel first, and then for the Church, Zion speaks of divine heritage, protection, and the joy of living under God's blessing. It is also a call to faithfulness: promised Zion implies a people who respond to the covenant.

sens: Ancestor of a family of temple servants
Chief of the temple servants at the time of Nehemiah
H6727G.detail: 1. Tsicha is the name of an ancestor whose descendants formed a family of Nethinim, that is, servants dedicated to the service of the temple in Jerusalem. After the exile in Babylon, his descendants are among those who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43). 2. Another Tsicha, or perhaps a descendant of the same name, was chief of the temple servants at Ophel (a hill in Jerusalem) during the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:46). These temple servants, although slaves or descendants of slaves, held an honorable role in the rebuilt religious community.
H6727G.origine: The Hebrew name Tsicha (צִיחָא) literally means "the dried up" or "the sunburned," evoking someone who is arid or dry. It is a symbolic or descriptive name, as was common in Israel, where names often carried a meaning related to the circumstances of birth or character. The exact meaning of this nickname escapes us, but it was borne by this important figure from the time of the return from exile.
H6727G.emploi: Tsicha appears twice in the Bible, always in relation to the Nethinim. First in Ezra 2:43, where his sons (his descendants) are listed among the families of temple servants who returned from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel, around 538 B.C. The same list reappears in Nehemiah 7:46, a few decades later, confirming the continuity of this family in the service of the temple in Jerusalem. It is a testimony to the organized structure of the restored community and the stable role of the servants of worship.
H6727G.portee: Tsicha represents the importance that God gives to all those who serve Him, even the humblest. These Nethinim, although servants, found a precise and honorable place in the restored faith community after the exile. Their presence in the return records shows that the reconstruction of God's people also included the material services of the temple — a lesson that no service to the Lord is insignificant.

sens: Chief of the Nethinim, that is, the temple slaves, at the time of Nehemiah
H6727H.detail: Tsicha is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:21. He is presented as one of the chiefs of the Nethinim — these servants dedicated to the service of the temple in Jerusalem — who lived on the temple hill (the Ophel district) after the return from exile in Babylon. His name literally means "dried up" or "arid" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a burned land or drought. Tsicha led these temple servants, alongside another chief named Guischpa.
H6727H.origine: The name Tsicha comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of dryness or aridity (something dried up). It is a personal name, with no direct grammatical or etymological link to other common biblical terms. This man was probably either a descendant of a family of Nethinim exiled in Babylon or himself a temple servant established after the return.
H6727H.emploi: Tsicha appears only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 11:21. This verse lists the chiefs of the Nethinim who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, when the people of Judah returned to rebuild the temple and the city. Tsicha and Guischpa are named as leaders of this community of temple servants, indicating that they were men of trust and authority in the reorganization of the religious life of Jerusalem.

sens: Wild creature that inhabits the desert or desolate places
Nomadic people or group living in arid regions
H6728.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a wild animal that lives in the desert: in Isaiah 13:21, we see the "desert animals" settling in the ruins of Babylon, alongside owls and ostriches. It is an undomesticated creature, symbolizing desolation and abandonment of a place.
2. By extension, it applies to the inhabitants of the desert, nomadic or semi-nomadic peoples who live in these inhospitable regions. Isaiah 23:13 mentions the "inhabitants of the desert," the Chaldeans who established their power in these arid lands. The word can also refer to enemies who, like wild beasts, bow down before God (Psalms 72:9).
H6728.origine: The root צִי (tsiy) evokes the hoarse cry and howling of wild creatures in the desert. The word belongs to the family of names for animals and living creatures in hostile environments. This root conveys the idea of primitive life, far from civilization and human protection.
H6728.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and in the Psalms. It often describes the desolate aspect of places once inhabited and prosperous: Babylon and Tyre, great cities, become dens for the "desert animals." In Psalms 72:9, the enemies of the king are compared to these creatures that bow the knee before him. The prophetic context uses this term to symbolize divine abandonment and the ruin of human power: where man and civilization once reigned, the wild beast and silence now dwell.
H6728.portee: This word reminds us that human power is fragile and that without God's favor, even the greatest cities fall into ruin and become dens of wild beasts. It invites the believer to recognize divine sovereignty over history and to seek not earthly glory, but the blessing of God, which alone ensures stability and prosperity.

sens: Instrument of captivity used to immobilize a prisoner
By extension, detention or imprisonment
H6729.detail:
1. Shackles are chains or metal restraints that were attached to the feet or wrists of prisoners to immobilize them and prevent escape. In Jeremiah 29:26, the priest must put "in prison and in shackles" anyone who falsely claims to be a prophet: the shackles symbolize here the concrete instrument of captivity.
2. The word can also refer to the state of detention itself, the deprivation of freedom. The shackles then represent the oppression and condemnation of the prisoner.
H6729.origine: The Hebrew word צִינֹק (tsinôq) literally refers to metal instruments used to restrain a captive. Its precise etymology is debated, but the image is that of a rigid object that constricts and paralyzes. The word belongs to the vocabulary of justice and punishment in the Old Testament.
H6729.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 29:26. It is used in a context of religious discipline: the high priest has the right to arrest and shackle anyone who claims to prophesy without God's mandate. The use of shackles reminds us of the seriousness of the penalty and the authority of the clergy to maintain order in the temple.
H6729.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible takes religious impostors and false prophecy seriously. The shackles also symbolize the concrete consequence of disobedience and lying: the loss of freedom. For the believer, it is an invitation to discern true prophets from false ones and to understand that God protects His people through order and legitimate authority.

sens: Fortified city of Judah in the mountainous region
H6730.detail: Zior is a small city mentioned in the distribution of lands of Judah after the conquest. It appears in a list of nine cities that Joshua 15:54 enumerates as belonging to the same territorial group as Hebron (Kirjath-Arba), in the mountainous region of the Negev. Its name literally means "smallness," suggesting that it was a modest urban center.
H6730.origine: The name Zior comes from a Hebrew root meaning "small" or "tiny." This name reflects the humble and small character of this locality compared to the larger cities of Judah like Hebron.
H6730.emploi: Zior appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:54, during the census of cities allocated to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. It is grouped with other small mountain towns in the region of Judah.

sens: Flower, bloom of a plant
Ornamental carving or engraving in the shape of a flower
Shiny gold plate on the high priest's diadem
That which shines, that which is bright and ephemeral
H6731A.detail:
1. The flower as a living part of the plant: it is the natural flower that blooms. Job 14:2 clearly states this by comparing the flower to fragile human condition: "He comes forth like a flower and withers away."
2. The decorative ornament in the shape of a flower, carved or sculpted: it can be found in the Temple at the House of the Lord, on the olive wood doors (1 Kings 6:32), where artisans shaped "blossoming flowers" in the wood, then covered them with gold.
3. The pure gold plate fixed on the sacred diadem of the high priest (Exodus 28:36): it is a band engraved like a seal with the words "Holiness to the Lord." Although the word means "flower," this plate was shining like a flower, hence this poetic name.
4. The image of that which shines but fades: Isaiah 28:1 speaks of the "fading flower" as a symbol of the superficial and fleeting glory of the drunkards of Ephraim, which will vanish.
H6731A.origine: The word צִיץ (tsits) literally means "flower" or "that which shines." It comes from a root that evokes the idea of sparkling or protruding. The word is related to צִיצָה (tsitsah), a feminine variant also designating the flower. This root reflects the biblical observation of the flower as something bright, visible, and remarkable in nature.
H6731A.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Tanakh. In the legal texts (Exodus and Leviticus), it specifically refers to the engraved gold plate of the high priest (Exodus 28:36, Leviticus 8:9), called the sacred diadem. In the description of the Temple (1 Kings 6), it refers to the floral motifs sculpted on the doors and walls, covered in gold (1 Kings 6:18, 6:32, 6:35). In biblical poetry and among the prophets, the word takes on a more abstract and melancholic tone: in Job (14:2) and Isaiah (28:1, 40:6-8), it embodies the fragility and fading of human glory and earthly beauty, a poignant contrast to the eternity of God.
H6731A.portee: This word teaches the reader two things: first, that all that shines and seems important in this world — crown, adornment, carnal beauty — withers and disappears like a flower, while God alone is eternal (Isaiah 40:7-8). Secondly, that the brilliance and ornamentation of the worship of the true God (the priest's diadem, the sculptures of the Temple) reflect a lasting holiness, in contrast to human vanity. It is a call to detach one's heart from passing glories.

sens: Member or appendage of the body allowing flight
Figuratively: rapid escape, fleeing
H6731B.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the wing of a bird or a winged creature, the organ that enables flight. This is the concrete and primary meaning of the word.
2. The Bible also uses it figuratively to evoke a rapid escape and fleeing: in Jeremiah 48:9, the command "Give wings to Moab" means "Make Moab flee quickly" — it is a poetic invitation to hasty flight. The image of the wing suggests the lightness and swiftness of one who escapes.
H6731B.origine: The Hebrew word צִיץ (tsits) is probably a variant or a rare form of the more common word for "wing." It conveys the idea of rapid and aerial movement. The poetic context and the image of flight dominate its biblical usage.
H6731B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 48:9. It is used figuratively and poetically to urge Moab to flee before divine judgment. The usage is metaphorical: giving wings means allowing or hastening an escape. This image emphasizes the speed and inevitability of disaster.
H6731B.portee: This passage shows how the Bible uses the image of the wing to express the urgency and inevitability of judgment. For the Christian reader, it serves as a reminder that the consequences of sin catch up with those who flee, and that no escape evades divine justice.

sens: Mountain pass near Tekoa, in Judea
H6732.detail: Tsits is a pass or narrow passage in the mountains that descend from the heights of Judea toward the Dead Sea. It is a strategically important military passage, close to the city of Tekoa. The only biblical usage shows it in the context of war: King Jehoshaphat is commanded to go meet a coalition of enemies by ascending the hill of Tsits to intercept them (2 Chronicles 20:16).
H6732.origine: The Hebrew word צִיץ (tsits) literally means "flower." Here it geographically designates a passage or mountain pass, likely named for a visible feature of the terrain or vegetation in that region near Tekoa, in Judea.
H6732.emploi: Tsits appears only once in the Bible. It is a geographical location mentioned during King Jehoshaphat's great victory over the Moabites and Ammonites, around 875 B.C. This event is reported in 2 Chronicles 20, and the passage through Tsits is described as the route by which the enemies were advancing to attack and where Jehoshaphat was to meet them.

sens: the colored and delicate part of a plant, which precedes the fruit
that which blooms and shines before fading away
the fragile and ephemeral brilliance of an ornament or beauty
H6733.detail:
1. The flower is the living and colorful part of a plant, the one that bears the promise of fruit but fades very quickly. In Isaiah 28:4, the prophet describes the faded "flower" of a crown, an image of royal beauty that withers in an instant.
2. By extension, the flower symbolizes everything that shines beautifully but lasts only a moment. It evokes deceptive brilliance, superficial glory that fascinates the eye but vanishes as quickly as it appears.
H6733.origine: This word is another form, very close, to the word tsits (צִיץ) which also means "flower." Both derive from a Hebrew root that paints the image of something that blooms and radiates before fading. The flower is the natural emblem of what bursts forth, shines, and then fades away.
H6733.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 28:4. The prophet uses it to describe a faded crown at the top of a fertile valley. Through this image of the withering flower, Isaiah denounces the ephemeral pride of those who trust in their wealth and beauty: all of this passes as quickly as a flower that is barely picked.
H6733.portee: This word invites the Christian not to cling to bright and fleeting appearances. It reminds us that true glory is not that which blooms for a moment on this earth, but that which is rooted in God. It teaches us the vanity of pride and the importance of grounding our lives on what lasts eternally.

sens: braided or threaded ornament at the edge of a garment
cord or tuft of threads
hair or lock of hair
H6734.detail:
1. A band of small threads or fringes that adorns the edge of a garment — it is a very visible decorative detail. In Numbers 15:38, God commands the Israelites to make fringes on the edges of their garments, with a blue cord in the middle, as a distinguishing sign of their identity as a chosen people.
2. By extension, a tuft or a set of threads braided or tied together, serving as an ornament or sign. Numbers 15:39 shows that this fringe is not just a decoration: it is a reminder — when seen, one remembers God's commandments and commits to follow them.
3. Literally, it can also refer to a lock of hair or a tuft of hair. In Ezekiel 8:3, God seizes the prophet "by the hair of his head" to take him away in vision, using the same word to refer to the hair or locks.
H6734.origine: The Hebrew word צִיצִת comes from a root that evokes the idea of tuft, lock, or something that hangs and sways. It designates both textile fringes (intentional construction) and hair (natural tuft). It is a word that paints a concrete visual image — something that is seen, that hangs, that attracts the eye.
H6734.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible. Twice in Numbers 15, in verses 38 and 39, where it describes the ordinance of ritual fringes on the edge of the garment as a sign and reminder of the commandments. Once in Ezekiel 8:3, in a very different context, where it simply refers to the hair of the prophet's head that God seizes. It is a concrete, less common word, linked to the religious identity of Israel and the visible distinction of its people.
H6734.portee: For the believer, the fringe serves as a reminder that God wants His word to be visible in our lives — not hidden, but manifested. This detail of the garment becomes a sign: every time we see it, we return to obedience and refuse to drift according to our own desires. It is a lesson in humility: we need external signs to remind us internally of our commitment to God.

sens: one who carries a message from one person to another
one who is sent on an official or diplomatic mission
one who conveys news
one who brings words or orders
H6735A.detail:
1. The messenger is primarily one who physically carries a message between two people: he goes from one to the other to convey what has been entrusted to him. In Proverbs 13:17, a wicked messenger "falls into misfortune" because he does not fulfill his task well, while a faithful messenger "brings healing," meaning he resolves conflicts by honestly conveying words.
2. The messenger can also be an official envoy, a kind of ambassador or agent assigned an important mission. In Isaiah 18:2, the king of Ethiopia sends "messengers" by sea to carry his words or orders to other nations.
3. One who brings news or information: in Jeremiah 49:14 and Obadiah 1:1, a "messenger" is sent to announce among the nations a decision or news (here, a command for war against Edom).
4. By extension, one who transmits requests, spices, or offerings, acting as an intermediary. In Isaiah 57:9, the nation sends "messengers" far away to fulfill its intentions.
H6735A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to send" or "to be sent." A messenger is therefore literally "one who is sent." The word belongs to the family of sending verbs, common in Hebrew to express the idea of mission or delegation. This notion of sending is at the heart of the role: the messenger does not act on his own but in the name of the one who sends him.
H6735A.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in contexts of transmitting important messages. It is particularly frequent in Proverbs and the prophets. In Proverbs 13:17 and 25:13, the messenger is praised for his faithfulness or criticized for his dishonesty: his honor and reliability are essential to his function. In the prophets (Isaiah 18:2, Isaiah 57:9, Jeremiah 49:14, Obadiah 1:1), messengers are diplomatic or political agents sent by kings or nations to communicate decisions of war or official orders. The context changes little of the meaning, but the solemnity grows with the stakes: from the simple bearer of words to the servant of a national or divine cause.
H6735A.portee: The biblical messenger reminds us that every person sent by God or serving as a relay between two others has a moral responsibility: they must be faithful, honest, and diligent. The figure of the messenger also shows that God Himself often acts through intermediaries — angels, prophets, disciples — who carry His message to the world. Understanding this role helps the reader to respect those who convey the Word of God and to be a messenger of truth themselves.

sens: metal piece fixed on a door frame, around which the door pivots
H6735B.detail: 1. A hinge is the metal (or reinforced wooden) piece that allows a door to turn on its frame. It is the axis around which the door articulates and opens or closes. In Proverbs 26:14, the text compares a lazy person lying in bed to a door that "turns on its hinges" — meaning it moves constantly but remains in the same place, without true progression.
H6735B.origine: The Hebrew word צִיר (tsir) literally designates what turns or pivots. It is related to the idea of rotation and articulation. It is a concrete word, borrowed from the daily life of the home: every door in ancient Judea rested on its hinges to function. The word appears only once in the Bible, in this figurative passage.
H6735B.emploi: The word צִיר appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 26:14. It is used metaphorically to illustrate the inertia of the lazy person. While a door that turns on its hinges changes its physical position with each rotation, the lazy person remains lying in bed — he has much apparent agitation, but no real action, no true change in his life. The image is vivid and striking for all readers who were familiar with the simple and daily functioning of a door.
H6735B.portee: This image of the hinge invites the reader to distinguish movement from true progress. It warns against activity that produces nothing — turning and turning without advancing. For the believer, it is an invitation to ensure that their agitation is not in vain, but that it bears fruit and produces true change in their life and that of others.

sens: violent spasm or contraction of the body, especially during childbirth
anguish or inner distress that grips the heart
